🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian. Published in Andishe Pouya 102

You have always said that spirituality is a process that brings tranquility, joy, and hope. As you pass seventy, have you yourself attained this tranquility, joy, and hope?

🔹As for tranquility, I am content and I believe I have it. As for hope, I am also content. But joy, no. From childhood onward, I think — perhaps due to my psychological makeup, or perhaps due to my childhood environment — I have fundamentally never been happy. This one thing I truly lack, and I have never truly laughed from the bottom of my heart; never.

Looking back on your life from the vantage point of seventy, what was the hardest period of your life? And what was the most precious price you paid for intellectual honesty?

🔹I think the most precious price I paid was losing friends. I am a person who cherishes friendship, and friendship matters greatly to me. To this day, I myself have never cut ties with anyone. But with every intellectual transformation I underwent, I lost a number of friends for whom I was very dear. It was as though their beliefs mattered more to them, and when I changed my beliefs, they would sever their friendship with me.

🔹The hardest period of my life was when I forsook many outward trappings and privileges in order to bring about, in my own estimation, a transformation in the Qom seminary. At that time I was also devout in every sense; out of compassion and mercy, I wanted the educational, training, and research system of the seminary to change so that the very goals they held would be realized and achieved in the best possible way. For example, I myself began changing the textbooks — that is, I was teaching, but not with the seminary textbooks, rather with books I deemed better. But gradually I saw that I was far too small to accomplish anything against this very old edifice. During those eighteen years in which I wanted to do something in Qom, I was awarded a scholarship twice to be sent abroad, and I went neither time. It always seemed to me that if this transformation took place in the seminaries, it would be more beneficial for society. But I returned unsuccessful. In the year 1372, after much pressure, I came and bought a house in Tehran and returned to Tehran to live. Again some of the gentlemen insisted that no, stay in the seminary. I gave back the very house I had bought in Tehran, and returned to Qom once more, staying there another seven years until the year 1379. But I saw that everything was falling apart.

🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves to have our present understanding. ✍Mostafa Malekian

Sometimes we look at the past and say: If I had spent those years doing something else, I would have a better life today. Why did I play so much as a child? Why did I pursue things in my youth that no longer matter to me today?

But in this judgment, we forget one thing: every period of life has its own demands. We cannot have had a childhood without having the interests and desires of childhood. We cannot have gone through youth and yet expect to have had our present maturity from the very beginning.

Part of our sorrow about the past comes from this very expectation — as if we wanted to have been as mature throughout our entire lives as we are today. Whereas it is precisely by going through those periods that we have reached this point.

▪️ Let us not see past mistakes as pure loss

Even a choice that we consider a mistake today may have brought us joys and friendships.

For example, we say, why did I pursue football instead of studying? But how much happiness has that same football given us? What friendships did it create that have stayed with us later in life?

If we only look at the costs of a choice and dismiss all the good things that came from it, we will not have a complete picture of the past.

▪️ No life is all benefit and no cost

Every way of life opens up possibilities before us and also carries costs. We cannot compare our lived life with an imaginary life that has all the good things and pays no price for them.

▪️ Let us seize the remaining opportunities

Not all opportunities are lost with the end of youth. There are still things we can begin, things we can learn, and pleasures we can experience.

If we spend today only on regret for yesterday, in a few more years, today will also become a new subject for regret.

Instead of only lamenting lost opportunities, let us treasure the opportunities not yet lost.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | Lecture on the book "Philosophical Guidance for Middle Age"

🔴 Four differences between morality and religious rituals and rites✍Mostafa Malekian🔹Why are religious rulings and rituals not among moral requirements? Because moral propositions and ritual religious propositions differ from one another, including:▪️ 1. Rational justificationMoral rulings are capable of rational justification; one can explain what effect observing or not observing them has on human life.For example, reason understands that lying destroys trust, misleads others in decision-making, and damages human relationships. But reason alone does not understand what problems human life in general would face if we did not perform wudu or tayammum.▪️ 2. The bond among human beingsMorality can serve as the basis of a shared system for the life of all human beings; a system that helps their coexistence and compatibility. But rituals and rites do not create such a universal commonality and can also mark the boundary between followers of different religions and sects.▪️ 3. Conscience versus instructionMorality is related to the inner conscience of the human being; a person feels within themselves that good is preferable to evil. But knowledge of rituals and rites depends on instruction and cultural transmission.Imagine a fourteen-year-old adolescent who has not received religious instruction: they can understand the meaning of honesty — that is, harmony among beliefs, feelings, desires, speech, and action — and grasp its value; but they do not know prayer, tayammum, or the Eucharist without instruction.▪️ 4. Stability versus historical dependenceMoral values are not specific to a particular time, geography, ethnicity, or nation; but the form of rituals and rites depends on historical and cultural contexts.For example, the form and limits of religious covering and what is considered hijab have not been the same in different periods and societies. Ways of worship also differ among religious traditions. But the value of honesty does not change with a change of clothing, land, or historical period; harmony of speech and action and not deceiving others still has moral value.➖An excerpt from a private conversation among friends - Dey 96@mostafamalekian

🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa Malekian

We usually assume that if good things happen to us, we'll feel good too. But the pleasantness of an event, in itself, doesn't guarantee that we can handle it well.

We live in a world that can be hard on us in two ways: not everything goes the way we want, and we have no certainty about what's coming.

▪️ The world has no obligation to fulfill our desires

There's no reason all the world's events should conform to our preferences and wishes. Some events are pleasant and some unpleasant; even a single event can make one person happy and another miserable.

Rain is a source of joy for a farmer waiting to water his field; but for a launderer who has hung washed clothes out to dry in the sun, it spells trouble.

The rain is the same rain; what differs is its relation to our desires and circumstances. The world has neither sworn to be our enemy nor promised to always go along with what we want.

▪️ Even joys may show up uninvited

The difficulty isn't just that we dislike certain events; it's also that we don't know what will come, or when.

Suppose you love someone dearly, but they show up at your door unannounced. Despite being happy to see them, you might lose your composure and fail to receive them the way you'd like.

Loving a guest is not the same as being ready for their arrival.

The same holds for the good things in life: we may want something, yet not be prepared for its sudden arrival. As a result, our reaction may be ill-considered and create fresh problems.

▪️ The suffering of the event and the suffering of the reaction

Part of life's difficulty comes from events not matching our desires; another part can stem from how we face them.

If we expect life to always unfold according to our wishes and predictions, we'll be constantly caught off guard. And being caught off guard can push us into reactions that only deepen our suffering.

So we must prepare ourselves to live in a world that holds both adversity and uncertainty—so that we can meet what arrives uninvited with greater composure.

We can't control the arrival of every uninvited guest; but we can learn how to face them.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | A conversation about the book "Welcoming the Unwelcome" by Pema Chödrön
